title: THE PROSTITUTES WERE GETTING INTO HEAVEN BEFORE THE RELIGIOUS LEADERS—AND JESUS SAID IT TO THEIR FACES.
paragraphs: THE PROSTITUTES WERE GETTING INTO HEAVEN BEFORE THE RELIGIOUS LEADERS—AND JESUS SAID IT TO THEIR FACES.

The shocking truth behind Matthew 21:28–32: Why the people everyone condemned were entering God's Kingdom ahead of those who believed they were already righteous—and why this warning may be closer to your own life than you think.
There are words Jesus spoke that comfort the broken.
There are words He spoke that healed the sick, restored the rejected, and gave hope to people who thought their lives were beyond repair.
And then there were words so piercing, so unsettling, so devastating to religious pride that they must have left an entire crowd struggling to breathe.
This was one of those moments.
Imagine standing in the temple courts of Jerusalem.
The religious leaders are there. Men respected by society. Men who know the Scriptures, observe religious traditions, and are accustomed to being treated as spiritual authorities.
They have spent years building reputations around their knowledge of God.
And standing before them is Jesus of Nazareth.
He looks directly at these respected religious authorities and says something almost unimaginable.
The tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the Kingdom of God ahead of you.
Not the priests.
Not the religious experts.
Not the people whose lives looked respectable from the outside.
The tax collectors.
The prostitutes.
The very people society had learned to despise.
And here is what makes this confrontation even more disturbing.
Jesus was not telling them that sin did not matter.
He was telling them that their religious appearance could not substitute for repentance.
The people they looked down upon had responded to God's call, while they themselves were resisting it.
And before you decide this story is about hypocritical religious leaders who lived two thousand years ago, consider something.

What if the most dangerous place for your soul is not where everyone can see your sin, but where you have become so comfortable with your religion that you can no longer recognize your need to repent?
Because that is where this story becomes personal.
Painfully personal.
And it begins with a father, two sons, and one simple command.
In Matthew 21:28–32, Jesus tells a parable about a man who had two sons.
The father approached the first son and told him to go work in the vineyard.
The son refused.
No beautiful promises.
No respectful religious language.
No attempt to sound obedient.
He simply said no.
But later, something changed.
He reconsidered.
He turned around.
And he went.
The father approached the second son with the same instruction.
This son gave the answer every father would want to hear.
He agreed to go.
His words sounded respectful. His response sounded obedient. His intentions, at least as expressed aloud, appeared honorable.
But he never went.
One son spoke rebellion and eventually obeyed.
The other spoke obedience and ultimately disobeyed.
Then Jesus asked the religious leaders which son had done the will of his father.
They answered correctly.
The first.
And that was when Jesus turned their own answer into a mirror.
Matthew 21:31 records His words in the King James Version:
"Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you."
Imagine the silence.
The leaders had understood the parable.
They had given the correct theological answer.
But they had failed to recognize that Jesus was describing them.
They were the second son.
The son whose mouth said yes while his life said no.
And the people they despised?
They were like the first son.
The ones who had lived in disobedience but were now responding to God's call.
This is where the original Greek makes the confrontation even more revealing.
In Matthew 21:31, the phrase translated "go into the kingdom of God before you" contains the words:
προάγουσιν ὑμᾶς εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ
proagousin hymas eis tēn basileian tou theou
A faithful rendering is:
"They are going ahead of you into the kingdom of God."
The verb proagousin comes from proagō, meaning to go before, precede, or lead ahead.
Jesus was describing a shocking reversal of expectations.
Those considered spiritually disqualified were responding to God's Kingdom message ahead of those who assumed they were closest to God.
Notice something important.
Jesus did not say that prostitution was righteous.
He did not say dishonest tax collection was acceptable.
He did not say morality was meaningless or that repentance was unnecessary.
He was confronting people who had mistaken religious status for genuine obedience.
The scandal was not that God had lowered His standard. The scandal was that notorious sinners were repenting while respected religious leaders refused to.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because the Gospel is not permission to remain in darkness.
It is the announcement that sinners can come into the light.
To understand why Jesus spoke so forcefully, we must look at what happened immediately before this parable.
In Matthew 21:23–27, the chief priests and elders challenged Jesus' authority while He was teaching in the temple.
Jesus responded by asking them whether John's baptism came from heaven or from human beings.
They refused to answer.
They understood the implications.
If they acknowledged John's ministry as coming from God, they would have to explain why they had not believed him.
If they dismissed John, they risked the reaction of the crowd, which regarded him as a prophet.
So they said they did not know.
Then Jesus told the parable of the two sons.
This was not an unrelated moral lesson.
It was a direct exposure of their response to God's messenger.
John the Baptist had come preaching repentance.
He had called people to turn from sin and prepare for the coming of the Lord.
And some of the people who responded were tax collectors and others whom respectable society regarded as deeply sinful.
Luke 3:12–13 records tax collectors coming to John and asking what they should do. John told them not to collect more than they were authorized to collect.
In other words, genuine repentance was not merely an emotional experience.
It demanded a changed relationship with sin.
Then Jesus explained the meaning of His parable in Matthew 21:32:

"For John came unto you in the way of righteousness, and ye believed him not: but the publicans and the harlots believed him: and ye, when ye had seen it, repented not afterward, that ye might believe him."
Read that final accusation again.
They had seen it.
They had witnessed people responding to God's call.
They had seen lives turning toward righteousness.
They had been given evidence that John's ministry was bearing the fruit of repentance.
Yet they would not repent and believe.
And perhaps those are the most frightening words in the passage.
Not because they describe people who had never heard the truth.
But because they describe people who had encountered the truth and still refused to surrender.
There is a Greek word in this verse that deserves our attention.
μετεμελήθητε — metemelēthēte
It comes from metamelomai, a verb that can express regret, a change of mind, or reconsideration.
In this context, Jesus rebukes the leaders because even after seeing the response to John's ministry, they did not reconsider their rejection and come to believe.
The same verb family appears earlier in the parable when the first son changes his mind and goes to work.
This connection matters.
The first son did not become obedient because his original refusal was harmless.
He became obedient because he changed his response.
The religious leaders, however, would not change theirs.

We should also be careful not to treat metamelomai as though it always means full biblical repentance. The word can describe regret without lasting spiritual transformation, as its use concerning Judas in Matthew 27:3 illustrates.
But in Matthew 21, the context connects a changed response with believing God's messenger and doing the Father's will.
The point is unmistakable.
God was not praising the first son's rebellion. He was showing that his refusal did not have to be his final answer.
And someone reading this needs to hear that.
Your first answer to God does not have to be your final answer.
Maybe you said no to Him when you were younger.
Maybe you ignored His Word.
Maybe you spent years doing things you knew were wrong.
Maybe you hurt people who trusted you.
Maybe you made choices that still haunt you when the house becomes quiet.
Maybe you carry a past you would never dare describe in front of your church.
And perhaps somewhere along the way, you began believing that your history had already decided your future.
But look at the first son.
He said no.
And later, he went.
His beginning was not the end of his story.
And in Jesus Christ, your past does not have to be the final word over your life.
That does not erase consequences.
It does not make wounds disappear overnight.
It does not mean forgiveness is something we can demand from people we have harmed.
But it does mean that God's mercy can meet a genuinely repentant sinner in the very place where shame says there is no hope left.
Now imagine one of the prostitutes who heard John's message.
We do not know her name.
We do not know her circumstances.
We do not know the details of her life, and Scripture does not give us permission to invent them.
But we know what Jesus said about people in that category who believed John's message.
They believed him.
Imagine the weight of that truth.
People who were accustomed to being judged by their reputations were responding to a call to righteousness.
Meanwhile, some of the very people expected to recognize God's work were rejecting it.
It is possible to know the language of holiness and still resist the Holy One.
It is possible to recognize sin in another person's life while carefully protecting it in your own.

It is possible to attend worship, memorize Scripture, defend sound doctrine, and become so skilled at appearing spiritually mature that you stop examining whether your heart is actually yielding to God.
That is not an argument against worship.
It is not an argument against studying Scripture.
It is not an argument against doctrine, holiness, or faithful church leadership.
All of those matter deeply.
But none of them can replace a heart that responds to God in faith and obedience.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable for people like us.
Because sometimes we are not the openly rebellious son.
Sometimes we are the son who knows exactly what to say.
We know when to say amen.
We know how to pray in public.
We know which Bible verses to post.
We know how to encourage people while privately refusing to deal with the very sin the Holy Spirit has been confronting in us.
We can say, "Lord, I surrender everything," while quietly keeping one part of our lives off-limits.
We can speak about forgiveness while nourishing bitterness.
We can speak about purity while entertaining secret compromise.
We can speak about generosity while refusing to show mercy.
We can speak about loving our neighbors while treating inconvenient people with contempt.
And we can become so accustomed to the sound of our own religious words that we mistake them for obedience.
That is the terrifying possibility Jesus exposed.
You can give God the right answer and still refuse Him your life.
Jesus expressed a related warning in Matthew 7:21:
"Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven."
The issue is not whether obedience earns salvation.
Scripture is clear that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of our works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
But the very next verse, Ephesians 2:10, says believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
We are not saved because we have successfully performed enough religious duties.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And that grace begins transforming the way we live.
Genuine faith does not make obedience unnecessary.
It gives obedience its proper place as the fruit of a life being changed by God.
This is why the message of Matthew 21 cannot be reduced to "bad people go to heaven and good people do not."
That would distort Jesus' teaching.
The deeper contrast is between those who respond to God's call and those who refuse it, regardless of their outward reputation.
A notorious sinner who repents is not beyond God's mercy.
A respected religious person who refuses to repent is not made righteous by public admiration.
And no one enters God's Kingdom simply because their sins were more dramatic, their suffering was greater, or their testimony was more emotionally powerful.
We all need the same Savior.
The tax collector needs Jesus.
The prostitute needs Jesus.
The preacher needs Jesus.
The church leader needs Jesus.
The person sitting quietly in the back row needs Jesus.
And the person reading this article, no matter how good or terrible their past may be, needs Jesus.
That is the beautiful offense of the Gospel.
It removes our ability to boast.
It also removes our reason to despair.
Because at the foot of the cross, neither religious achievement nor a shameful history can replace the need for Christ.
Romans 3:23 tells us that all have sinned and come short of the glory of God.
Romans 3:24 immediately speaks of sinners being justified freely by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
Do you see the movement?
From guilt to grace.
From condemnation to redemption.
From the truth about our sin to the greater truth about what God has done through His Son.
This is why Jesus' words were not simply a public humiliation of the religious authorities.
They were also a warning that demanded a response.
The leaders were not being told that repentance was impossible for them.
They were being confronted because they would not repent.
Their position was not their salvation.
But neither did their position make them unreachable by grace.
They too needed to turn and believe.
And perhaps that is the invitation hidden inside the confrontation.
Jesus exposes what is false so that people can turn toward what is true.
He confronts self-righteousness because self-righteousness blinds us to our need for mercy.
He calls sinners to repentance because sin destroys, deceives, and separates us from the life for which we were created.
He does not tell us the truth to entertain our shame.
He tells us the truth because He is the Savior who came to rescue sinners.
And the rescue came at an unimaginable cost.
The One speaking in the temple would soon be betrayed.
Condemned.
Mocked.
Crucified.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, would give His life for sinners.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because sin was so serious that our redemption required the saving work of Christ.
As 1 Peter 2:24 says, He bore our sins in His own body on the tree, so that we might die to sins and live unto righteousness.
And the cross was not the end.
Jesus rose from the dead.
The Savior who calls sinners to repent is the risen Lord who offers forgiveness and new life.
This is the heart of Christianity.
Not respectable people congratulating themselves for being better than everyone else.
Not broken people being told their sins do not matter.
But guilty people being offered mercy through the crucified and risen Christ, and being called to follow Him.
Grace does not tell you to make peace with the chains that are destroying you. Grace brings you to the Savior who can set you free.
Maybe this is why the story of the two sons is so difficult to forget.
Because the question is not merely which son we resemble.
It is what we will do now.
Will we keep giving God beautiful words while resisting His will?
Or will we finally turn toward Him?
Maybe you have been saying you will forgive someone, but you keep feeding the bitterness.
Maybe you have been promising to leave a destructive habit, but you keep returning to it in secret.
Maybe you have been delaying an honest confession because you are afraid of what people will think.
Maybe you have been avoiding church because someone who claimed to represent Jesus wounded you deeply.
Maybe you have confused the failures of Christians with the character of Christ.
Or maybe you are the person everyone admires.
The reliable one.
The faithful one.
The person people ask to pray.
And yet somewhere beneath the ministry, the responsibility, and the reputation, your heart has grown cold.
You still know the songs.
You still remember the verses.
But you cannot remember the last time you approached God without pretending.
If that describes you, this passage is not an invitation to perform another religious act so that you can feel better about yourself.
It is an invitation to come honestly before the Lord.
To stop defending what He is calling you to surrender.
To stop hiding behind what other people think of you.
To stop treating repentance as something only the obviously sinful need.
And to remember that the mercy of Jesus Christ is not exhausted by the truth about your life.
There is a remarkable promise in 1 John 1:9:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Not because confession purchases forgiveness.
Not because we can repair ourselves through sufficient remorse.
But because forgiveness rests on the faithful and righteous work of God through Jesus Christ.
And the invitation to repent is not limited to people with scandalous pasts.
It reaches the respectable.
The successful.
The religious.
The disappointed.
The exhausted.
The ashamed.
The ones who have been pretending.
The ones who have stopped praying because they do not know what to say anymore.
And the ones who think they have already gone too far.
If that is you, listen carefully.
The first son changed his response.
And the father had not withdrawn the command.
There was still a vineyard.
There was still an opportunity to obey.
There was still a meaningful difference between refusing and turning.
But do not misunderstand this as a promise that we can delay repentance indefinitely.
Scripture repeatedly warns us against hardening our hearts.
Hebrews 3:15 says:
"To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts."
Today matters.
Not because you can force yourself into salvation through emotional intensity.
But because the proper response to God's truth is not endless postponement.
It is faith.
Repentance.
Surrender.
And trust in Jesus Christ.
Perhaps the prayer you need today is not eloquent.
Perhaps it sounds something like this:

"Lord Jesus, I have spent too much time trying to look right instead of being honest before You. I have defended things I should have surrendered. I have judged people whose struggles were visible while hiding my own. Forgive me. I cannot save myself. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Teach me to trust You, turn from sin, and follow You with a heart that truly belongs to You. Amen."
And if that prayer reflects what is happening inside you, do not let this moment disappear beneath the next notification.
Take time with the Lord.
Open Matthew 21:28–32 for yourself.
Read it slowly.
Ask what God is exposing in your heart.
And then respond.
Not merely with words.
With faith that begins bearing fruit.
There is something else I want you to remember.
Somewhere in your life, there may be a person you have quietly written off.
Someone with a terrible reputation.
Someone who has made destructive choices.
Someone whose past makes you uncomfortable.
Someone you assume would never listen to the Gospel.
But Matthew 21 should make us cautious about deciding who is beyond the reach of God's grace.
You do not know what God may already be doing in that person's heart.
You do not know whether someone you consider far from God is beginning to seek Him with greater honesty than people who have spent decades around religious activity.
That does not mean we ignore sin.
It means we refuse to treat sinners as disposable.
It means we speak truth without forgetting mercy.
It means we remember that Jesus came to seek and save the lost, as Luke 19:10 declares.
Not to accuse them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to suggest that you are spiritually superior.
But because there may be a person on your Facebook friends list who has been quietly wondering whether Jesus could ever receive someone with their past.
Send it privately to someone who may not be comfortable discussing their struggles publicly.
And if this passage has confronted something in your own heart, I would genuinely love to hear what it has stirred in you.
You do not have to reveal private details to strangers. Even a few sincere words can become an opportunity for fellow believers to encourage one another in prayer.
And if you have experienced the mercy of Christ after a season of rebellion, your testimony may remind someone else that repentance and restoration are possible.

Not because these words are more important than Scripture, but because you may need to return to Matthew 21 on a day when religious pride, shame, or discouragement tries to distort your understanding of grace.
At Gospel Warrior, this is why we keep sharing the Word of God.
Not to build a community around personalities.
Not to turn the Gospel into a product.
And certainly not to make anyone believe they can purchase God's favor.
We want to see people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ, grow in biblical understanding, repent where repentance is needed, find encouragement in God's promises, and become more faithful disciples.
These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, strengthen their faith, and continue learning about Jesus Christ.
Your local church, family responsibilities, and thoughtful stewardship matter.
And never believe that your standing with God depends on a payment.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"God loveth a cheerful giver."
It is the opportunity to help sustain a community devoted to biblical truth, encouragement, discipleship, and the proclamation of Jesus Christ.
Pray for this ministry.
Read and share the Scriptures.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Jesus Christ is not a reward for those who can afford a monthly contribution.
He is the Savior who freely receives sinners who come to Him in faith.
And that brings us back to the temple.
Back to those religious leaders.
Back to the tax collectors and prostitutes.
Back to the two sons.
One said no and later obeyed.
One said yes and never went.
The religious authorities knew which son had done the father's will.
But knowing the right answer did not mean they had responded rightly to God.
And now the question stands before us.
Not as a clever religious puzzle.
Not as an excuse to condemn the Pharisees from a comfortable distance.
But as a question that reaches into our private lives.
Have we mistaken knowing about God for knowing Him?
Have we confused religious language with surrender?
Have we judged other people's visible sins while excusing our own hidden disobedience?
And most importantly, what will we do with the truth now that we have heard it?
Jesus did not come merely to improve the reputation of sinners.
He came to save them.
He did not die so that we could keep pretending we were righteous without Him.
He died and rose again so that sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed by His grace.
That is why no scandalous past should make you believe that repentance is pointless.
And no respectable present should make you believe that repentance is unnecessary.
The invitation is the same.
Come to Christ.
Believe His Gospel.
Turn from sin.
Receive His mercy.
And follow Him.
Because when Jesus said the tax collectors and prostitutes were entering God's Kingdom ahead of the religious leaders, He was not celebrating how far those sinners had fallen.
He was exposing how dangerous it is to refuse the grace that calls us to rise.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth of all is this:
The first son was not defined forever by the day he said no—and the second son was not made obedient by the day he said yes.
What mattered was the response that followed.
So do not spend your life trying to convince everyone that you have already said yes to God.
Come to Jesus with an honest heart.
And follow Him.
The tragedy is not that your past once said no to God. The tragedy would be hearing His call today and still refusing to come home.
